bugs: Nothing limits how long the job can keep retrying (no retryUntil). With #[Tries(10)], Backoff up to 300s and 429 releases of up to 600s each, a job can run past the 15-minute claim. The dispatcher then treats the rows as abandoned and dispatches them again, so they are pushed twice. The stale job's failed() can also clear the new job's claim (app/Jobs/PushStockAllocations.php:16,49,71).
The claim UPDATE in the chunkById callback does not re-check readiness or lock rows. It is only safe because of onOneServer (app/Console/Commands/DispatchStockSync.php:20-23).
The 429 handling only reacts after the fact. Nothing throttles the requests, so about 50 jobs hit a slow API at once and every 429 uses up one of the 10 tries.
antipatterns: app/Providers/AppServiceProvider.php:23 Schedule::useCache('redis') hardcodes the store name. The default cache is already Redis in production.
app/Jobs/PushStockAllocations.php:16 sets a fixed Tries(10) alongside releases on 429. A rate-limited job should be bounded by time (retryUntil), not by a try count.
strengths: synced_at is captured before the read and every update goes through toBase(), so an edit made while the request is in flight stays ready. The probe confirmed this.
Caps the Retry-After delay at 600 s and sends the job's writes in one transaction.
The whereNotNull('sync_started_at') guard makes a redelivered job do nothing.
Good, focused Pest tests with describe blocks, including idempotency, 429 handling via a Job mock, and an edit after the read.

bugs: Retry-After is not capped (app/Jobs/PushStockAllocations.php:47). A large value (the probe used 3600) sends the job past retryUntil, so the job fails and the rows wait for the next dispatcher run. Nothing is lost, but the backoff is not handled well.
The two marking updates are not wrapped in a transaction (lines 58-61). This is minor.
There is no throttling before requests are sent, so all jobs hit the slow API at once at peak volume.
antipatterns: app/Jobs/PushStockAllocations.php:41 uses a hard-coded timeout(30) inline. This is acceptable but inconsistent with the attribute-driven config used elsewhere.
app/Jobs/PushStockAllocations.php:23 returns the FQCN \DateTimeInterface instead of importing it.
strengths: retryUntil is tied to CLAIM_TTL_MINUTES - 1, so a job always gives up before its claim counts as abandoned. A test enforces this.
The claim runs in a transaction with lockForUpdate and a limit(100) loop, which is safe even without onOneServer.
Uses partition() to split missing from accepted rows, and toBase() keeps updated_at untouched.
synced_at is the time before the read, so an edit made mid-request is not lost (verified by probe).
Lean code. The tests are clear, including a travel()-based test for an abandoned claim and a failed()-then-dispatch round trip.

bugs: synced_at is set to coalesce(sync_started_at, now()), the claim time. An edit made between the claim and the job's read is pushed, but the row still counts as ready and is pushed a second time. No data is lost.

The default RateLimited limit of 30/min is an invented number (config/services.php). RateLimited also releases jobs without capping them against retryUntil, but the 10-minute window easily covers about 50 jobs.
antipatterns: app/Jobs/PushStockAllocations.php:75 interpolates a string into raw SQL: DB::raw("coalesce(sync_started_at, '{$fallback}')"). The value is safe today, but this is a pattern to avoid.
app/Models/StockAllocation.php:12 makes the internal sync-state columns (sync_started_at, synced_at, disabled_at) mass-assignable through #[Fillable].
tests/Feature/StockSyncTest.php:239-245 has a weak rate-limit test that only checks that middleware and a limiter exist.
strengths: The only implementation that throttles before sending: RateLimited('storefront') middleware backed by the shared Redis limiter, plus reactive handling of 429 via $response->tooManyRequests().
Clamps Retry-After to 30-300 s within a 10-minute retryUntil, so a job finishes or fails well before the 15-minute claim expires.
The claim uses a transaction, lockForUpdate and a limit loop. The job's writes are in a transaction and touch only the batch's own rows.
Tests use withFakeQueueInteractions()->assertReleased(), freezeTime and travel. They cover idempotency, editing after a claim, and failed() round trips.
The service URL and limit live in config.

bugs: A lost update. $syncedAt = now() is taken after the rows are read (app/Jobs/PushStockAllocations.php:39-50). An edit made between the read and that line sends the old quantity, but synced_at is later than updated_at, so the change is never pushed. A probe that edits in the retrieved event confirmed this. The comment on line 49 claims the opposite.
Retry-After is not capped (line 59). The probe got a 3600 s release, far beyond retryUntil, so the job fails and the rows wait for the next dispatcher run.
There is no throttling before requests are sent.
The endpoint is hardcoded as a class constant instead of coming from config/services.
antipatterns: app/Jobs/PushStockAllocations.php:18-25 uses public $tries/$maxExceptions/$timeout/$backoff properties instead of queue attributes, and $tries = 0 is ceremony when retryUntil is set.
app/Models/StockAllocation.php:31 uses the legacy scopeReadyToSync instead of #[Scope], and line 18 uses protected $fillable that includes the sync-state columns.

app/Models/StockAllocation.php:11 adds #[UseFactory], and StockAllocationFactory.php:11 adds $model. Both are redundant with HasFactory naming conventions. The definition also sets columns that default to null.
app/Jobs/PushStockAllocations.php:55 builds sku/quantity with a manual map closure where map->only() would do.
tests/Pest.php:19,22 uses inline FQCNs instead of imports. .env.example was edited for deployment concerns.
strengths: The claim runs in a transaction with lockForUpdate, a limit loop and an empty-check short-circuit.
The job skips rows that are no longer claimed or are disabled, so a redelivered job does nothing.
retryUntil(10 min) stays shorter than the claim TTL, and a test enforces it.
Tests are split per unit and cover 429, 500, failed() and abandoned claims.

v.rationale:
All four test suites pass (impl-1: 20, impl-2: 16, impl-3: 24, impl-4: 17). I ran four throwaway probes against each implementation and then deleted them: an edit made while the job reads the rows, a 3600 s Retry-After, a full dispatch-and-sync cycle followed by an edit and a second dispatch, and a 500 error that makes the job give up.

**impl-3 ranks first.** It is the only one that fits the task's load profile: a slow API, 429 responses, about 5,000 rows and Redis as the shared cache. It throttles requests before sending them through RateLimited middleware on the shared Redis limiter, and it also handles 429 responses after the fact. It keeps Retry-After within 30–300 s and ends retries at 10 minutes, so a job finishes or gives up before its claim expires. Rows are claimed under a lock in a transaction. Its weaknesses are a raw-SQL string interpolation and a harmless extra push of rows edited between claim and read.

**impl-2 ranks second.** It is the leanest of the four. It claims rows correctly under a lock, ties retryUntil to the claim lifetime, uses partition() well and passed the edit-during-read probe. It does not cap Retry-After and does not throttle requests before sending.

**impl-1 ranks third.** It has the best modern idioms and records the sync time correctly. However, it limits the job by a try count (10 tries) and sets no time limit. With backoffs and 429 releases of up to 600 s, a job can outlive its 15-minute claim, so the dispatcher sends the same rows a second time. That breaks the requirement to send each change exactly once.

**impl-4 ranks last.** The probe confirmed a real lost-update bug: it records the sync time after reading the rows, so an edit made between the read and that line is never pushed. It also uses the most legacy idioms (property-based job config, scopeX, protected $fillable, a hardcoded endpoint, a redundant UseFactory), leaves Retry-After uncapped, and has a confused updated_at test assertion.
